node.label: Maxine Berg
node.date_label: The Age of Manufactures (1985; second edition 1994) · A Woman in History (1996) · Luxury and Pleasure (2005)
node.description: Maxine Berg argues that industrialisation grew through varied forms of manufacture and the labour of women and families, rather than being adequately explained by factories and aggregate growth alone, in The Age of Manufactures (1985; revised 1994). Luxury and Pleasure in Eighteenth-Century Britain (2005) connects Asian luxury imports, demand among middling consumers and new products to industrialisation. Joyce Burnette noted its attention to consumer goods often ignored in accounts of the Industrial Revolution. With Pat Hudson, Berg also challenged aggregate measures of industrial change and later argued that slave-based Atlantic demand stimulated skills and innovation. A Woman in History (1996) recovered Eileen Power’s comparative economic history and examined its gendered remembrance. Helen Mellor praised the biography but questioned whether its medieval-history chapter adequately established Power’s historical achievement; Berg answered that collaborative work and comparative method mattered beyond major monographs.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Machinery Question and the Making of Political Economy (1980); The Age of Manufactures (1985; second edition 1994); A Woman in History: Eileen Power, 1889–1940 (1996); Luxury and Pleasure in Eighteenth-Century Britain (2005); Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution (2023), with Pat Hudson.
node.scope_note: Monographs not read in full. The Power preface and October 1996 review/response were read; Luxury arguments use the publisher abstract and Burnette’s displayed extract. Selected passages of the 1990 working paper, 2017 conference paper and 2021 joint article were read. The 1992 journal article, full Burnette/North reviews and 2024 reply remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Who Made Luxury” (2017), Berg credits de Vries’s industrious-revolution work as an influence on her Luxury Project.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed 27, introduction: “greatly influenced”; 30 discusses The Industrious Revolution (2008). This is Berg’s retrospective attribution; de Vries’s book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Berg’s preface to A Woman in History (1996) credits Thomas’s 1989 suggestion for her turn to biography.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Preface xiii, paragraph 1: “I owe this change in my approach”. Specific suggestion, not supervision. Biography chapters unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Suggestion to write the Power biography

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Woman in History (1996), Berg recalls using Clark’s books while researching women’s and family labour for The Age of Manufactures (1985).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Preface xiii: “drawn back to books written by Alice Clark” and others. Clark’s particular title unspecified; no exclusive debt asserted.
proposed_edges.map_label: Earlier women economic historians as resources

proposed_edges.relationship: A Woman in History (1996) credits Davis’s “History’s Two Bodies” (1988) with helping Berg’s early writing.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Preface xiv, final paragraph and note 2 continuing xv: “Two key articles helped me”. Davis’s essay unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: History’s Two Bodies as a resource

proposed_edges.relationship: In her response concerning A Woman in History (1996), Berg defends Power’s comparative programme and collaborative scholarship as achievements obscured by monograph-centred judgments.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: October 1996 response, paragraphs beginning “Major monographs” and “The Wool Trade”: “not the only measure”. Biographical interpretation, not personal contact; full book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Pat Hudson, Berg’s “Slavery, Atlantic trade and skills” (2021) challenges Mokyr’s supply-side explanation, locating stimuli for skill formation in slave-based Atlantic trade.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher PDF 260–261, 275–276: “On this we agree” accepts skilled workers’ importance. Their objection concerns timing, regional concentration and stimuli; Mokyr’s original unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Atlantic demand versus a supply-side explanation

proposed_edges.relationship: With Pat Hudson, Berg’s “Rehabilitating the Industrial Revolution” working paper (1990) challenges causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s national demographic series.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed 30–33, Demography: “aggregative studies”. They retain local variation and Schofield’s revised interpretation. Joint critique; not rejection of reconstruction itself. 1992 journal version unread. Existing edge_1084 mediates this criticism through capitalismdebates; no direct Berg–Wrigley edge exists.
proposed_edges.map_label: Aggregate series and regional demographic causes

proposed_edges.relationship: Luxury and Pleasure in Eighteenth-Century Britain (2005) links demand for new middling-class consumer goods with product invention and industrialisation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher book abstract, final sentence, read in the record for the 2007 manifestation; original year from Warwick and Burnette. Full book unread. Existing roster concerns the separate Clifford coedited collection.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her response about A Woman in History (1996), Berg explains how women, feminism and internationalism shaped early economic history and how gendered remembrance diminished Power’s scholarship.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: October 1996 response, paragraphs beginning “In contrast” and “She may have built”; “female scholar rather than for the history”. Full biography unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Women and the discipline’s historical memory

proposed_edges.relationship: “Who Made Luxury” (2017) connects Asian exports and production knowledge with European imitation, manufacture and changing consumption.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed 28–30, Luxury and the East: “provided models” and discussion of knowledge conveyed by traded goods. Argument read; underlying eighteenth-century accounts not independently examined.
proposed_edges.map_label: Asian production within global consumption history

proposed_edges.relationship: With Pat Hudson, “Rehabilitating the Industrial Revolution” (1990 working paper) contests growth accounting as a sufficient measure of industrial transformation, stressing innovation, women’s and children’s labour and regional change.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed 4–5: “mis-specified”; four areas stated on 5. Joint argument, read in 1990 version; journal article (1992) unread. Existing edge_1083 is an economic-field route; this adds its named coauthor’s route.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘The Rhetoric of Chartist Domesticity’ (1992), Anna Clark applies an argument from Berg’s The Machinery Question and the Making of Political Economy 1815–1848 (1980) to explain how treating women’s and children’s work as a moral problem could shield political economy from criticism and make Chartist domestic rhetoric politically vulnerable.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher PDF’s opening and selected substantive passages, especially printed pp. 82–85 and notes 112 and 124. Clark names Berg in the body, applies her analysis to the vulnerability of Chartist domesticity, and identifies the cited work through the two notes. This is substantive uptake, not an inference from a reference list. Clark expressly says Berg was discussing another context; the edge therefore claims application rather than attributing Clark’s account of Chartism itself to Berg. Berg’s cited p. 296 was not independently read. Original article publication is January 1992, not the publisher’s 2014 online posting. Anna Clark is a run member, distinct from Alice Clark, whose pair is already in the supplied input.
proposed_edges.map_label: Applies Berg’s analysis of labour, morality and political economy (1992)

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Machinery Question and the Making of Political Economy 1815–1848 (1980), Berg contributes to the history of technology by distinguishing contemporaries’ identification of industrialisation with machinery from the limited geographical and industrial spread of mechanisation and the continuing expansion of manual production.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete publicly displayed Introduction summary and publication metadata, plus the publisher summary of chapter 2, ‘The progress of the machine’ (pp. 20–31; DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511560330.004). The Introduction contrasts the public identification of industrialisation with machines and the concentration of actual mechanisation in relatively few industries and regions. Chapter 2 states her project of charting mechanisation as the basis for examining contemporary ideas. History of technology is an editorial mapping to this documented intervention; no claim of founding the field or of later scholarly adoption follows from the summaries. The book body remains unread. This target is an existing field endpoint and is absent from the supplied Berg pair list; its prior roster mention does not constitute a direct edge.
proposed_edges.map_label: Distinguishes machinery’s public meaning from its uneven spread (1980)
